## Solution

**No, $f$ does not necessarily have a (unique) fixed point.**

### Uniqueness holds whenever a fixed point exists

First, observe that if a fixed point exists, it is automatically unique. Suppose $p \neq q$ are both fixed points: $f(p)=p$ and $f(q)=q$. Then

$$d(p,q) = d(f(p),f(q)) \geq L\, d(p,q) > d(p,q),$$

a contradiction. Hence at most one fixed point can exist.

### A fixed point need not exist (counterexample)

Take the complete metric space $X = [0,\infty)$ with the usual metric $d(x,y)=|x-y|$ (this is a closed subset of $\mathbb{R}$, hence complete). Define

$$f(x) = 2x + 1.$$

**Well-definedness as a self-map:** For every $x \geq 0$, we have $f(x) = 2x+1 \geq 1 \geq 0$, so $f:X\to X$.

**Expansive condition:** For any $x \neq y$ in $X$,

$$d(f(x),f(y)) = |(2x+1)-(2y+1)| = 2|x-y| = 2\,d(x,y),$$

so the condition $d(f(x),f(y)) \geq L\,d(x,y)$ holds with $L=2>1$.

**No fixed point:** Solving $f(x)=x$ gives $2x+1 = x$, i.e. $x = -1$, which does not belong to $X=[0,\infty)$. Therefore $f$ has no fixed point at all.

### Conclusion

The expansive condition $d(f(x),f(y)) \geq L\,d(x,y)$ with $L>1$ on a complete metric space does **not** guarantee the existence of a fixed point. The map $f(x)=2x+1$ on $X=[0,\infty)$ is an explicit counterexample. (Note: the condition does force $f$ to be injective, and the inverse $f^{-1}:f(X)\to X$ is a contraction with ratio $1/L$; but since $f$ need not be surjective, $f^{-1}$ need not be a self-contraction on all of $X$, so the Banach fixed point theorem cannot be applied to guarantee a fixed point.)
